stanzas: Isa! Isa! vulagi lasa dina
Nomu lako au rarawa kina
A'cava beka ko a mai cakava?
Na nomu lako, au na sega ni lasa.
Isa Lei na noqu rarawa,
Ni ko sa na vodo ena mataka
Bau nanuma tiko ga,
Mai Suva, nanuma tiko ga.
Vanua rogo na nomuni Vanua
Kena ca ni levu tu na ua
Lomaqu voli me'u bau butuka
Tovolea ke balavu na bula.
Vanua rogo na nomu yanuyanu
Kena kau wale na Salusalu,
Mocelolo, Bua, na Kukuwalu,
Lagakali, baba na rosi damu.
orig.credit: Traditional; the Fijian text as quoted in Wikipedia's article

stanzas: Isa! Isa! visitor who truly gladdened [?],
your going, I grieve over it.
What was it, perhaps, that you came to do [?]?
At your going I shall not be happy.
Isa Lei, my sorrow,
when you will go aboard in the morning,
just keep remembering,
keep remembering Suva.
A famous land is your land,
its one fault is that the waves are big;
my heart longs [?] that I might tread on it,
I will try, if life is long.
A famous land is your island,
its plants are nothing but garlands [?]:
mocelolo, bua, kukuwalu,
lagakali, and beside them the red rose.

notes: line 1.1 and 2.1: 'Isa' (fuller 'Isa lei') is a cry of longing and sorrow, kept as it stands; 'vulagi' is a visitor or stranger, 'lasa' joy or delight, 'dina' true: the phrase is read here as 'a visitor who truly brought joy', but the grammar is uncertain.
line 1.3: 'A cava beka', 'what, perhaps'; the line reads as a reproach, 'why ever did you come?'.
line 2.2: 'vodo', to board a ship or vehicle.
line 2.4: 'Mai Suva' could also be 'here at Suva', the singer's place.
line 3.3: 'Lomaqu voli', 'my wish, my longing'; 'voli' is uncertain here.
line 4.2: 'kau' is tree or plant; 'wale', merely; 'salusalu', garland: the island's plants are all fit for garlands.
lines 4.3-4.4: mocelolo, bua (frangipani), kukuwalu and lagakali are fragrant Fijian flowering plants used in garlands; they are kept as names. 'baba' is the side or edge.
